claims.claim: Lessard, quoted in Ryan, contrasts template-driven retrieval with the historians' practice of letting the archive speak.
claims.source: James Ryan, 'Curating Simulated Storyworlds', PhD dissertation, UC Santa Cruz, Dec 2018

claims.claim: Tarn Adams says a whole class of Dwarf Fortress players skip both play modes and instead do archaeology on the worlds they have generated, reading the history in Legends mode.
claims.source: Tarn Adams, interviewed by Wes Fenlon, 'Dwarf Fortress creator Tarn Adams talks about simulating the most complex magic system ever', PC Gamer, 16 Mar 2017
claims.quote: They just do archaeology on the worlds they've generated
claims.page: body, section on the four modes

claims.feature: other: generated history that does not reach the present
claims.claim: Tarn Adams says many things that happen in world generation do not get pushed forward, leaving stories that cannot continue, and calls that bad.
claims.source: Tarn Adams, interviewed by Wes Fenlon, 'Dwarf Fortress creator Tarn Adams talks about simulating the most complex magic system ever', PC Gamer, 16 Mar 2017
claims.quote: you have these stories that can't continue, which is bad
claims.page: body, on carrying world-generation events into play

claims.claim: Tarn Adams says the named objects Dwarf Fortress dwarves had made for eleven years were not that interesting, though they existed and had names, until claims and history were attached to them.
claims.source: Tarn Adams, interviewed by Wes Fenlon, 'Dwarf Fortress creator Tarn Adams talks about simulating the most complex magic system ever', PC Gamer, 16 Mar 2017
claims.quote: They're not that interesting, but they're there, they have names

claims.feature: other: derive the system from the world's premise
claims.claim: Tarn Adams says deriving magic from each world's generated creation myth gives a deeper connection than a fixed ladder of level one and level two spells.
claims.source: Tarn Adams, interviewed by Wes Fenlon, 'Dwarf Fortress creator Tarn Adams talks about simulating the most complex magic system ever', PC Gamer, 16 Mar 2017
claims.quote: There's a deeper connection than just, this is your level one spells
claims.page: body, on myth generation and magic

claims.claim: Tarn Adams says a random generator would be very hard-pressed to capture really beautiful symbolism or an advanced writing device.
claims.source: Tarn Adams, interviewed by John Harris, 'Interview: The Making Of Dwarf Fortress', Gamasutra, 27 Feb 2008
claims.quote: You'd be very hard-pressed to capture really beautiful symbolism

claims.feature: other: elicit the human process first
claims.claim: Tarn Adams describes his generation method as finding the key basic elements, finding the rules that govern them, and activating them in the world.
claims.source: Tarn Adams, interviewed by John Harris, 'Interview: The Making Of Dwarf Fortress', Gamasutra, 27 Feb 2008
claims.quote: finding the key, basic elements, finding the rules that govern them

claims.feature: other: generated detail must be load-bearing
claims.claim: Mark R. Johnson says Ultima Ratio Regum foregrounds generated civilizational, cultural and religious detail in its actors rather than leaving such content as background or lore, as many games do.
claims.source: Mark R. Johnson, 'Modelling Cultural, Religious and Political Affiliation in Artificial Intelligence Decision-Making', AISB 2015 AI and Games symposium
claims.quote: rather than leaving such content as "background" or "lore"
claims.page: section 2, Procedural Generation and Artificial Intelligence

claims.feature: other: generated detail must be load-bearing
claims.claim: Mark R. Johnson says the generated cultural backgrounds are the only route by which his actors' motivations, interests and agendas can be understood.
claims.source: Mark R. Johnson, 'Modelling Cultural, Religious and Political Affiliation in Artificial Intelligence Decision-Making', AISB 2015 AI and Games symposium
claims.quote: whose motivations, interests and agendas can only be understood
claims.page: section 2, Procedural Generation and Artificial Intelligence

claims.feature: other: typed pools of world facts
claims.claim: Mark R. Johnson says a URR algorithm can procedurally create over a million detailed religions carrying beliefs, gods, festivals, eschatology and altar appearance.
claims.source: Mark R. Johnson, 'Modelling Cultural, Religious and Political Affiliation in Artificial Intelligence Decision-Making', AISB 2015 AI and Games symposium
claims.quote: procedurally create over a million detailed religions
claims.page: section 2, Procedural Generation and Artificial Intelligence

claims.claim: Mark R. Johnson reports over 1 trillion possible generated AI actors in URR, and rests the claim of difference on their behaving differently by social and cultural context rather than on the count.

claims.page: section 2, Procedural Generation and Artificial Intelligence

claims.feature: other: every varying feature carries a fact
claims.claim: Mark R. Johnson says a bookmark on a generated URR book shows a scholarly nation, one of several visual features that each encode a fact about the book's nation of origin.

claims.feature: other: sifting only finds what it was told to find
claims.claim: Kreminski and colleagues describe a simulated storyworld's output as a profusion of events, many of which are relatively uninteresting as narrative building blocks.
claims.source: Max Kreminski, Melanie Dickinson and Noah Wardrip-Fruin, 'Felt: A Simple Story Sifter', ICIDS 2019
claims.quote: a profusion of events, many of which are relatively uninteresting

claims.claim: Kreminski and colleagues report that they found it very difficult to anticipate in advance the full range of questions a sifting-pattern author would want to ask about the game state, and so gave authors a real query language instead of a preauthored function library.
claims.source: Max Kreminski, Melanie Dickinson and Noah Wardrip-Fruin, 'Felt: A Simple Story Sifter', ICIDS 2019
claims.quote: very difficult to anticipate in advance the full range of questions
